Three separate missing capabilities (auth-freshness reporting, secret typing, post-injection form-state verification) all show up in one five-call sequence, and the user's own CLAUDE.md now encodes the hazard as a rule ('never in fill or run-code', 'don't snapshot between fill and submit'). No JS dialog, cookie banner, download or upload appeared in any of these six sessions - the frictions that actually fired were tab identity, origin drift, secret typing, session expiry, and page-text extraction.

Six sessions, three of which actually drove cuttle (S36, S37 and S40 drove logged-in sites). Patterns visible only across them:

1) NOT ONE CDP INPUT EVENT WAS EVER SENT. Across all three cuttle sessions there is zero `click`, zero `type`, zero `fill`, zero `press`. Every interaction was a page load plus `eval`/`fetch`. cuttle's most expensive and most distinctive feature - humanized Input (curved mouse, log-normal keystrokes, typo injection, ~0.5s/click, ~130ms/char) - was exercised exactly never. In practice these agents used cuttle as "a logged-in cookie jar reachable over CDP", and two of three sessions bypassed the DOM entirely by calling the site's private API from inside the page. If that is representative, the cheapest wins are on the data-extraction and session-state axes, not the input-realism axis.

2) NOBODY EVER TOOK A SCREENSHOT - and two sessions hand-rolled a substitute. S36 built `location.href + body.innerText.slice(0,400)`; S40 read a driver-written `.yml` accessibility snapshot off disk. The recurring first question is always "where am I and what is showing", and there is no cuttle answer to it, so each session invents a different one. A single `cuttle peek` (url + title + text/aria digest, per tab) would have served all three.

3) THE LOGIN BOUNDARY IS THE ONLY PLACE HUMANS ARE STILL REQUIRED, AND IT IS UNINSTRUMENTED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. Before the handoff the agent cannot ask "is this origin still authenticated" (S36 wrote a site-specific `fetch('/api/retail/user/current/wallet')` probe); after it, the agent cannot detect completion and has to end its turn waiting for the human to type "its logged in". cuttle already stores per-seed auth snapshots - surfacing `auth status` and a blocking `wait-login` would close both halves and make unattended runs possible.

4) THE ATTACH/BRIEFING PATH IS GENUINELY GOOD - ZERO FAILURES. `cuttle up`/`status` printed the drivers, versions and exact attach commands, and every session attached correctly on the first try; there was not one failed cuttle or driver call in the entire batch (the only tool failures were Beeper 400s and a python typo). The friction is never "the command errored", it is always "the capability does not exist, so I wrote a workaround". Workarounds observed: innerText-slicing eval, private-API fetch replay, a bespoke `CUTTLE_CDP=... python` scraper (documented in the repo because "agent-browser's daemon socket cannot" carry a large return), giant shell-escaped JS piped through `jq -r .` into scratchpad files.

5) `cuttle up` IS NOT IDEMPOTENT-FEELING. The same command printed "already running", "running" and "restarted" across the three sessions; only the restart case silently discarded the tab set, and it gave no reason. Since this user habitually leaves logged-in tabs in the shared browser, a silent restart is real state loss with no notice.

6) TWO NON-DRIVING SESSIONS STILL SHOW CUTTLE COSTS WORTH KNOWING: in S39 the cuttle container measured 26-32% of a host core (roughly two-thirds of all OrbStack CPU) during a local performance investigation, and in S38 a local paid smoke reported bare 502/503 on the a link-aggregator site and a large e-commerce site endpoints purely because the cuttle sidecar was not running locally - no error anywhere said "cuttle unreachable", so the agent first read it as a payment regression. A clearer upstream-unavailable signal from the cuttle client would have saved that misattribution.

Four of the six sessions in this batch never drove a browser at all - two Go code reviews of a cuttle diff, one cloakbrowser source analysis, one skills review - and a fifth was a meta-audit reading someone else's browser session. Only one session (S12) actually attached to cuttle. That ratio is itself a signal: the cuttle corpus is dominated by reasoning ABOUT cuttle rather than driving it, so friction evidence is concentrated in a handful of long sessions and is easy to miss.

Three independent threads in this batch converge on ONE root cause - focus/visibility of the target tab. (a) Session 5 proves cuttle's base Chrome args are a byte-identical copy of the deployed daemon's 8-flag list and omit Playwright's four backgrounding switches, so a background/occluded renderer never fires rAF and Playwright's 'stable' actionability check can never satisfy. (b) The audited session in #2 shows the agent-facing symptom twice: a 5000ms click timeout on a button the driver had already resolved, escalating through force-click and dispatchEvent (~10 calls, and the synthetic fallback silently did not persist). (c) The same audited session shows a second symptom of the same family - document.visibilityState 'hidden' broke IntersectionObserver lazy-loading and cost 8 calls of phantom debugging. The daemon's per-page Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled pin evidently does not cover either case. This is the single highest-leverage fix in the batch.

The window/viewport contract is broken from both ends and nobody owns it. Session 1 measured drivers overriding cuttle's careful sizing (Playwright viewport 1920x1080 vs a macOS seed whose screen is at most 1728 wide - inner > screen on 5/5 macOS seeds, 3/4 Windows seeds). Session 3 found the opposite failure in the daemon (a seed hashing to 2560x1440 launches --window-size=2560,1392 on a fixed 1920x1080 Xvfb, ~1.7x raster memory off-screen). Same seam, opposite directions, both invisible at runtime.

Every capability gap shows up as an invented workaround, and the workaround is the feature request: three throwaway TypeScript probe scripts written into the user's repo to answer 'did the page render' (missing screenshot/page-state verb); a shell for-loop doing scroll+capture (missing scroll-sweep); in-page fetch against a site's own API returning 5.5 KB in one call where clicking would have taken 50 (missing 'read behind a login' pattern); a driver-specific PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_SECRETS_FILE env var as the only safe way to type a password (missing cuttle-owned secret injection, and it silently does not apply if the agent picks the batched-JS verb).

Success strings lie in three different places and only vision catches it: `agent-browser upload` returned '✓ Done' three times on a no-op; `tab new` returned '✓ Screenshot saved' for an unreachable URL; a probe run reported '-> ok' on six navigations that all died on net::ERR_INVALID_AUTH_CREDENTIAL. In each case the disproof was a post-condition read or a screenshot. Any cuttle write verb should return the post-condition, not a checkmark.

The human's complaints are never about a single slow call - they are about browser-driving as a mode ('i hope it would be faster and less error-prone', 'every time i ask you to check a professional social network, do you need to run cuttle for that?'), and both times he proposed the correct alternative himself before the agent found it.

STRUCTURAL NOTE FIRST: only 2 of the 4 assigned sessions have browser content, and neither drove a browser itself - both (S16 and S16) are friction-audit subagents spawned by the same parent in a project directory on 2026-08-08. This exact audit has already been run once. The primary sources are S06, S03, S24 and S05 - go to those for raw evidence, and do not double-count these two entries with any other analyst covering the same source ids.

PATTERN 1 - the single warm shared browser is the #1 failure mode, and it is invisible from both ends. Two independent sessions on two different days hit it: in S05 the human was browsing a SaaS console in the same Chrome she had just told the agent to use ('I'll do verification myself, meanwhile could you please use cuttle...'), and 13 straight coordinate clicks landed on her tab until she hit interrupt; in S06 a *second Claude session* stole the foreground and the human had to explain it ('there was a small interruption of another session using cuttle too'). `tab-select` reports `(current)` while `visibilityState` is `hidden`, so the driver's notion of 'current tab' and the browser's foreground are different things nothing surfaces. This is the highest-leverage fix in the whole batch: foreground/attached-client state in `cuttle status` and in every driver result, plus bringToFront guidance.

PATTERN 2 - silent success is worse than failure. Across all four source sessions the costly loops are the ones where an action returned a success-shaped result and changed nothing: CodeMirror inserts that exit 0 with the buffer unchanged, `el.click()` on a cloud provider's account chooser returning 'clicked account' with the URL unmoved, `click \"\"` on an empty ref no-opping, a bash ref-loop printing three empty arrows. Every one of these cost 10-20 calls because the agent had to invent its own verification eval. cuttle already has a settle gate and aria-toggle post-click verify - extending 'verify the mutation actually happened, else report failure' to fill/type would kill the largest single category of waste.

PATTERN 3 - blindness. S05 took ZERO screenshots in 183 browser calls and never once opened or mentioned the VNC viewer that `cuttle up` had printed for it, even when handing the task back to the human; S06 took 2 in 123. In both, one image at the moment of the third failed hypothesis would have ended a 13-call and a 9-call dead end. There is no `cuttle screenshot` verb, and nothing in the flow nudges an agent to look. 'When two consecutive actions produce no state change, look at the screen' is a one-line SKILL.md rule worth more than most features.

PATTERN 4 - inline JS in a shell argument is broken in every driver. playwright-cli run-code (21 of 40 calls written to a file), agent-browser eval (regex flags mangled by escaping, then 9 throwaway .js files), and S05's /tmp/inspect3.js, /tmp/usercap.js, /tmp/userhtml.js etc. Three different agents on two drivers independently invented the identical `cat > /tmp/x.js <<'EOF' ... EOF` workaround. Document the heredoc/--filename pattern as the default and the whole class disappears.

PATTERN 5 - no wait-for-condition, so agents sleep. 894s of sleep in S06 plus 7 hand-rolled polling loops (~40 min), 354s across 86 sleeps in S05, 602s of cold-start sleep in S03, and agent-browser padding `sleep 8` on top of its own `wait --load networkidle`. Notably nobody ever misread humanized input as a hang - the slowness complaints are about polling and cold start, not about the 0.5s click.

PATTERN 6 - the CLI's own lifecycle verbs get bypassed. S03 ran 413 Bash calls, 13 `docker run -d` and 21 defensive `docker rm -f`, and never once called `cuttle up`/`down`/`open`. When an agent is testing an image it reaches for docker directly and then reimplements port-conflict and readiness handling badly. `cuttle up --image` needs to be the documented path AND needs to block until CDP is genuinely ready.

PATTERN 7 - the browser's most reliable use turned out to be as an authenticated fetch origin, not a clicking surface. Both S24 and S06 abandoned a stuck UI widget and got the exact answer instantly via in-page `fetch()` (`200 :: {...}`, `409 {\"error\":\"This repository has already been submitted...\"}`, `429 rate_limit_exceeded`); S05 twice bypassed a dead DOM by hitting the app's own URL directly. Three agents rediscovered this independently. Worth promoting to documented practice rather than leaving as a last resort.

NEGATIVE FINDINGS worth recording: across all four source sessions there were ZERO cookie-banner fights, ZERO captcha/Cloudflare walls, ZERO shadow-DOM blindness in Angular Material, ZERO JS dialogs, and ZERO driver-spawns-its-own-browser attach failures. The persistent profile did its job - the agents were already logged into a cloud provider, a note-taking app and an internal tool. The real blockers were focus, shell quoting, cold start and unverified mutations, i.e. ergonomics, not stealth.

These two sessions ran CONCURRENTLY against the same cuttle browser on 2026-08-07, and neither agent ever realised the other was an agent. Session S05 saw a SaaS console tabs appear and concluded "something else is driving that browser" then "we're both driving the same browser"; session S06 saw a note-taking app/a cloud provider/an internal tool tabs appear and concluded "another session has opened tabs in this browser and stolen document focus". Each blamed the human. Both lost work: S05 abandoned a fully filled a note-taking app OAuth form and handed the task back to the user for two hours; S06 had its CodeMirror config corrupted into invalid JSON. cuttle ships `--context` and `context ls|add` for exactly this, and NEITHER session used them - because `cuttle up`'s briefing never mentions contexts, and its only concurrency guidance is "NEVER launch your own browser", which reads as a warning against a second browser, not a warning about a second driver. That single omission is the most expensive documentation defect visible across the batch.

Second cross-session pattern, equally sharp: screenshot usage is pure luck. Same model, same machine, same day, same driver, same user. Session S06 took 2 screenshots in 117 browser calls and both times it immediately resolved an ambiguity. Session S05 took 0 in 183 calls and instead authored 132 bespoke JavaScript DOM-scraping programs, 27 getBoundingClientRect coordinate computations, and 21 raw mousemove/mousedown/mouseup gestures - it rebuilt a vision-and-click system in JS because nothing in cuttle's briefing suggests looking at the page is an option. cuttle owns a KasmVNC framebuffer and has no screenshot verb; the briefing's only visual affordance is "hand the user the viewer link", which frames seeing the screen as a human activity rather than an agent one.

Third: both sessions independently discovered that input does not go where the driver thinks it goes, and neither could get a truthful answer about it. S05 found `visibilityState: hidden` and correctly inferred the foreground rule after three separate episodes. S06 found `document.hasFocus(): true` and was actively misled - it published a root cause it could not have verified. Those two signals disagree specifically because cuttle pins `Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled` per page. A cuttle feature intended to keep background tabs alive has made the standard agent focus diagnostic unreliable, and there is no cuttle-provided replacement.

Fourth, quieter: neither session ran `cuttle skill`. Both went straight to the driver's own SKILL.md. The briefing lists the driver docs command inline with the attach command and relegates the cuttle guide to its last line. Every cuttle-specific gotcha in this batch - foreground input routing, shared-browser collisions, snapshot leaking secret values via aria-label, the about:blank keep-alive tab occupying an ordinal - was rediscovered empirically at a cost of 60+ turns, and all four are things a guide could have stated in four lines that nobody read.

Three patterns only visible across both sessions:

(1) FRICTION IN THE CLICK PATH SILENTLY DISABLES CUTTLE'S CORE VALUE. In both sessions the driver's high-level click/fill no-opped on non-native widgets (Angular in the tax portal, React on a professional social network), and in both the escape hatch was raw in-page JS: 65 acting `eval` calls in session 1, 22 plus 28 synthetic-MouseEvent dispatches in session 2. In-page `el.click()` / `dispatchEvent` / native-value-setter never touches CDP Input, so cuttle's humanizer, settle gate, typo injection and post-click aria verify are all bypassed - exactly on the hardest pages, and with no signal that it is happening. Whatever else is fixed, the click path needs a humanized force-click so agents never have to reach for `eval` to act.

(2) READING STATE COSTS MORE THAN CHANGING IT. Session 1: 261 snapshots + 145 read-only evals = 46% of 892 calls. Session 2: 199 read-only evals + 29 snapshots. Neither session trusted the a11y snapshot for form state; session 1 escalated all the way to a file round-trip (save draft -> `cuttle downloads` -> grep XML) as its only believable ground truth, ~14 times. A `cuttle state`/`read` verb returning form values keyed by stable ids would collapse the single largest cost in both transcripts. The related tell: screenshots were used 9 times in 892 calls in session 1 and only after the user demanded it, because the output path had to be discovered by grepping driver stdout.

(3) EVERY BOUNDARY CROSSING IS UNDOCUMENTED AND WAS DISCOVERED THE EXPENSIVE WAY. Host filesystem -> container (both sessions independently ran `docker cp` into the cuttle container, and in both cases the host-side path would have worked); container -> host network (`host.docker.internal` failed, dev server had to be rebound to a LAN IP); driver -> driver (a beforeunload dialog owned by one driver session wedged the other, and the second driver's error blamed the tab); identity -> identity (the agent launched a non-cuttle browser for a second login until the user pointed it at `cuttle up --name`); and browser session -> site session (cookies persist, server sessions expire, and nothing surfaces the difference - it cost a lost multi-step wizard and nearly cost a lost tax declaration). Every one of these is a cuttle-layer concern that no driver can fix, and each was learned by burning turns rather than by reading SKILL.md.

Also worth noting for the human-handoff design: across both sessions the human took the keyboard/mouse in the viewer at least four times (typed a a national tax id, dragged a slider, entered credentials twice) and every single time the agent was blind to it until told in chat. cuttle sits between the viewer and the browser and is the only component that could report 'the human just acted'.

Three patterns visible only across the pair:

1. **The stealth invariant one session fought for, the other destroyed with one convenience call.** Session S03 spent an entire release cycle establishing per-seed screen/window coherence (dropping the 2560x1440 pair, pinning taskbar height, adding dropMaximizeIfSized, regenerating the golden) because "outerWidth 1536 around innerWidth 780 isn't a windowless launch, it's a visibly impossible window." One week later, session S04 ran `playwright-cli resize 1440 900` to make a screenshot look nicer, never restored it, and did all its logged-in work in that state. Nothing rejected it, warned, re-applied the seed size, or logged it. cuttle treats window geometry as identity on the way in and as a free-for-all on the way out.

2. **Users are maintaining a private cuttle cookbook because the product has no memory, and the cookbook is leaky by construction.** `a project directory/pjs/career/CLAUDE.md` now carries two hand-written "platform ops (cuttle browser)" sections (a freelance marketplace, Aug 5-6; a freelance marketplace, Aug 14). Most of their content is *generic cuttle knowledge*, not site knowledge - "ASSUME LOGGED OUT", "Drive the API, not the DOM", "mint the TOTP and submit in ONE chained command", "modals cache their data, RELOAD after an API write", "file input index 0 vs 1, then Crop". And three lines in the a freelance marketplace section are near-miss credential-leak rules the user had to derive alone: "`run-code` ECHOES ITS SOURCE to stdout, so any secret-bearing run-code would leak", "Do NOT snapshot the page between fill and submit (nothing auto-redacts the field value in snapshots)", "playwright-cli 0.1.17 removed `process` from the run-code sandbox, so the old process.env fill is dead". SKILL.md covers the happy path of secrets; every sharp edge around it was found the hard way, per user, per site.

3. **Both sessions failed the same way: they trusted a check that silently returns the wrong answer, and only caught it by luck.** S03 trusted `document.fonts.check()` (unpatched, returns true for everything) and published a wrong font finding; it also trusted a mid-run pod sample and published "panic confirmed fixed" two minutes before the daemon panicked. S04 trusted a `PATCH .../skills` that returned 200 and changed nothing, and trusted `x.thumbnail`/`x.images` field names that do not exist. In every case the recovery was the same discipline - "read state back after you change it" - which is already in SKILL.md and is the single highest-value line in it. The gap is that cuttle offers no primitive that makes read-back cheap: no `cuttle verify`, no crash counter, no per-seed status. The agents are doing verification by hand-built probe, and getting it wrong at roughly the rate you would expect.

4. **Minor but consistent: neither session ever encountered a JS dialog, and neither ever opened the VNC viewer voluntarily.** The one human handoff that happened (session 2's resume swap) was initiated by the human rejecting a tool call, not by the agent asking. The viewer is cuttle's headline human-in-the-loop feature and it appeared zero times in 250 browser turns.

session_summaries_deidentified.session_summary: Career research session that used cuttle for three browser jobs: filing an abuse report to a note-taking app about a malicious page, an API sweep of a freelance marketplace via in-page fetch, and a full email-OTP login to a talent-network site followed by editing and saving the user's live profile (bio, roles, skills, proof-of-work link, two references).
